title: Principles to help combat AI bias, security risks, and issues of meaningful consent affecting vulnerable populations
html:
As the attention to and the delivery of Artificial Intelligence (AI) enabled solutions continue to grow, so do the questions related to bias in the technology. How do we know if the black box will respond ethically? How do we know that these systems will guarantee the security of the vulnerable population (physical & virtual)? How do we know if the programmers were diverse enough to ensure that their product treats everyone fairly? Is there even a way to determine if bias occurred? These questions and concerns have grown so prevalent that new startups, like ORCAA, have been formed to perform algorithm audits and provide certifications.

When Jasmine Wright joined me this past summer, we discussed the topic of AI; the challenge of introducing it into the humanitarian sector carefully and ethically; and how it would be different than the private sector AI concerns and principles (Google AI principles & Microsoft AI principles). Of course, AI is already being used in several humanitarian context - both directly and indirectly. Looking at these early implementations, we can already learn how to improve future AI-enabled solutions. And, we can formulate humanitarian-specific principles on how AI should be used when working with the most vulnerable populations of the world.  

Over the course of three months, Jasmine conducted 20 interviews with a diverse range of experts in the AI and humanitarian fields and read through a significant number of scholarly and news articles. Leveraging this knowledge and insights, we have produced a report entitled Artificial Intelligence Principles for Vulnerable Populations in Humanitarian Contexts.

[PDF]

This report argues that AI systems with prevalent biases, security risks, and consent issues can undermine the role of humanitarian actors in disaster contexts by leaving aid recipients at further risk of vulnerability. The report proceeds in five sections: (a) examples of AI systems that are used for vulnerable populations (b) analysis of different forms of bias pertaining to AI systems, © evaluation of security risks, (d) examination of issues of consent over data collection, and finally (e) AI principles and recommendations specific to vulnerable people in the humanitarian field. 

These resulting principles are: 

  1. Weigh the benefits versus the risks: Avoid AI if possible
  2. Use AI systems that are contextually-based
  3. Empower and include local communities in AI initiatives
  4. Implement algorithmic auditing systems

Logically, such principles are only good if followed by organizations who work in or support the humanitarian sector. We hope that by releasing our report, along with suggested principles, an honest discussion can begin within and between organizations working on AI that relates to the most vulnerable people in the world.

Andrej

P.S. After our writing completed, the Pentagon announced its draft AI ethics guidelines to fight bias and rogue machines [PDF]
teaser: Principles proposed after 20 expert interviews by researcher Jasmine on AI bias, security risks and meaningful consent for vulnerable populations.
seo_description: Proposed humanitarian principles for AI that serves vulnerable people, covering bias, security and consent, based on interviews and scholarly sources.
